title: Spin Lock
body:
A lock you wait for by **busy-waiting**: sit in a loop testing the flag over and over until
it goes free. The waiting thread stays [[Process State|Running]] and holds the CPU the
entire time it is doing nothing.

[[TAS]] is the canonical one. That inner `while (tas(&lock)) ;` with the empty body is the
spin:

```C
while (tas(&lock))   // spin: keep testing until it comes back 0
    ;
// critical section ... ;
lock = 0;
```

[[Peterson's Solution]] spins too, on `while (flag[j] && turn == j);`.

## When spinning is actually right

The obvious objection is that it wastes CPU, and usually it does. The case for it is that the
alternative is not free either. Blocking means two [[Context Switching|context switches]]: one
to get off the CPU into a [[Wait Queue]], one to come back. If the lock is held for less time
than those two switches cost, spinning wins outright.

| | Spin | Block |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting thread's state | Running, burning CPU | [[Waiting state\|Waiting]], off the CPU |
| Cost to wait | proportional to how long you wait | two context switches, fixed |
| Good when | wait is very short, and there is another CPU | wait is long or unknown |
| Bad when | wait is long, or single core | wait is shorter than the switch |

**On a single core, spinning on a lock held by another thread is a hang**, not a delay. The
holder cannot run to release it while you are sitting on the only CPU testing the flag; you
just spin until the timer [[Interrupts|interrupt]] preempts you.

## Where the hardware comes in

The test and the set have to be one indivisible operation, or two threads both read 0 and
both think they won. That is not something software can arrange, so it needs an atomic
instruction from the CPU: [[TAS]], compare-and-swap, or the 68000's `tas`. See
[[Interrupts]] and [[Concurrency]] for the hardware side of why a two-instruction sequence
is not safe.

This is why kernels use spin locks and user code mostly does not. Kernel critical sections
are short, often run with interrupts disabled, and cannot always block. User code has
[[Mutex Lock|mutexes]] and [[Semaphores]] instead.
